title: Map Sum Pairs
description:
# Map Sum Pairs

Design a `MapSum` class that stores string keys with integer values and can return the sum of values for all keys that start with a given prefix.

Implement the `MapSum` class:

*   `MapSum()` initializes the object.
*   `void insert(String key, int val)` inserts the key-value pair. If `key` already exists, its old value is replaced by `val`.
*   `int sum(String prefix)` returns the sum of all values whose keys start with `prefix`. If no key has that prefix, return `0`.

A key may also be a prefix of other keys. In that case, `sum(key)` includes the value stored at the key itself and the values of longer keys below it.

A prefix is a contiguous beginning of a string. For example, `"ap"` is a prefix of both `"apple"` and `"app"`, but `"pp"` is not.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example:

**Input**
["MapSum", "insert", "sum", "insert", "sum"]
[[], ["apple", 3], ["ap"], ["app", 2], ["ap"]]

**Output**
[null, null, 3, null, 5]

**Explanation**
MapSum mapSum = new MapSum();
mapSum.insert("apple", 3);
mapSum.sum("ap"); // returns 3
mapSum.insert("app", 2);
mapSum.sum("ap"); // returns 5 because both "apple" and "app" start with "ap"

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= key.length, prefix.length <= 50`
*   `key` and `prefix` consist of lowercase English letters.
*   `1 <= val <= 1000`
*   At most `50` calls will be made to `insert` and `sum`.

tests.description: Canonical sequence where two keys share prefix `ap`.
Overwriting an existing key must replace its value instead of adding a second copy.
A prefix with no matching keys returns zero.
A prefix may itself be a full key and still include longer keys below it.
Independent trie branches and missing branches are both checked.
Updating one key in a shared prefix should adjust only that key contribution.
Repeating the same key with the same value must not double count it.
Nested one-letter prefixes verify exact prefixes at every depth.
A substring in the middle of a key is not a prefix.
Keys ending in `z` exercise the lexicographic upper-bound trick used by TreeMap solutions.
Updating a key that is also a prefix should preserve descendant contributions.
Long shared prefixes verify overwrite deltas deep in the trie.

solutions.name: Trie with Delta Prefix Sums
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store all keys in a trie. Every trie node keeps the sum of values for keys passing through that prefix. A separate hash map stores the current value for each full key. When `insert(key, val)` is called, compute `delta = val - oldValue`, then add that delta to every trie node along the key path.

## Key Insight

Updates are replacements, not additive inserts. The delta map is what keeps prefix sums correct when an existing key changes value or is inserted again with the same value. After the trie has stored prefix totals, `sum(prefix)` only needs to walk to the prefix node and return its cached sum.

## Complexity Analysis

Let `L` be the key length and `P` be the prefix length. Insertion costs `O(L)` and sum costs `O(P)`. The trie stores at most one node per distinct key character, so the space is `O(K * L)` for `K` keys plus the key-value map.

solutions.name: Prefix Sum HashMap
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain two maps: one from full keys to their current values, and one from every prefix string to the current sum for that prefix. On insertion, compute the replacement delta for the full key. Then generate every prefix of `key` and add the delta to that prefix's stored sum.

## Key Insight

This is the same delta idea as the trie solution, but it materializes prefix strings directly in a hash map. That makes `sum(prefix)` a single lookup. It is simple and very fast for the small official constraints, while also showing that the real challenge is handling replacement updates correctly.

## Complexity Analysis

Insertion touches all `L` prefixes of the key, so it costs `O(L)` hash operations, ignoring substring copy costs. `sum` is `O(1)` expected time. The prefix map stores up to `O(K * L)` distinct prefixes.

solutions.name: HashMap Brute Force Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store only the current value of each full key in a hash map. `insert` is a plain replacement. For `sum(prefix)`, scan every stored key and add the values of keys whose string starts with the prefix.

## Key Insight

This route is the clearest correctness baseline. It naturally handles overwrites because the map always contains only the latest value for each key. It is slower for many calls, but it makes the required semantics obvious before introducing cached prefix totals.

## Complexity Analysis

Insert is `O(1)` expected time. Sum scans `K` keys and each `startsWith` check may inspect up to `P` prefix characters, so it is `O(K * P)`. Space is `O(K)` for the key-value map.

solutions.name: TreeMap Prefix Range
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log K) insert, O(log K + R) sum
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store key-value pairs in a `TreeMap`, which keeps keys in lexicographic order. All lowercase keys with prefix `p` lie in the range `[p, p + "{")`, because `{` comes immediately after `z` in ASCII. `sum(prefix)` iterates over that sub-map and adds the current values.

## Key Insight

This solution avoids a trie but still uses the structure of strings. A prefix corresponds to a contiguous lexicographic interval. The upper bound must be chosen carefully; `prefix + "{"` works for lowercase English letters and correctly includes keys ending in `z`.

## Complexity Analysis

Insert costs `O(log K)`. Sum costs `O(log K + R)`, where `R` is the number of keys inside the prefix range. Space is `O(K)` for the ordered map.
